metadata.h1: Telecom Site Civil Construction in Kenosha, Wisconsin
metadata.intro: Kenosha is the southern gate of Wisconsin's busiest infrastructure corridor. Microsoft bought 240 acres at I-94 and WIS 142 in January 2025 with a four-building data center campus in mind, the Mount Pleasant campus sits one county north, and the 107-acre Kenosha Innovation Neighborhood is turning the old Chrysler engine plant site into mixed-use ground. The dirt under all of it is Lake Michigan lake plain — clayey till and glacial lakebed deposits over Silurian dolomite — and every foundation goes at least 48 inches down under the state frost rule. CellSite Solutions runs this market from Cedar Rapids, 234 road miles west, self-performing hut pads, duct bank, grounding, and compound civil across Kenosha County.

geotech.dominantGeology: Kenosha County occupies the Lake Michigan lake plain. Silurian dolomite bedrock lies roughly 25 to 50 feet below the surface across much of the county, capped by clayey glacial till with pockets of lacustrine (glacial lakebed) silt and clay; the shoreline north of the city rises into clayey bluffs up to about 35 feet high near the Racine County line. (City of Kenosha comprehensive plan resource inventory; USGS state geologic compilation for Kenosha County; WGNHS preliminary bedrock geologic map of southeastern Wisconsin.)
dominantSoilTypes: Clayey glacial till of the lake plain

karstRisk.note: No Kenosha County karst mapping was sourced during research. The Silurian dolomite here generally sits 25–50 ft down — below telecom foundation depths — but include a karst screen in any geotech scope with deep foundations or dewatering, since karst is documented in the same dolomite elsewhere in eastern Wisconsin.

geotech.foundationApproachNarrative: The Kenosha foundation conversation starts with clay and ends with the calendar. Lake-plain till and lakebed deposits hold water, so open excavations that would drain overnight in sandy ground stay wet here, and subgrades rut fast once disturbed — pump capacity and crushed-stone working pads earn their keep on most sites. Because the dolomite typically sits 25 to 50 feet down, rock rarely complicates a hut footing or shelter pier; what governs instead is Wisconsin's 48-inch frost embedment, which fixes the excavation depth on every foundation regardless of load. Spread footings and thickened pads below frost handle most telecom structures in this soil, with helical or drilled options reserved for bluff-adjacent or soft lakebed pockets. Borings decide, not the county map — order them early.

regulatory.permitTimelineNarrative: Plan a Kenosha schedule around three separate clocks. The building permit clock runs through the city's Building Inspection Division under the statewide SPS code, with state plan review layered on for larger structures. The ROW clock is the city's two-step Public Works process — registration on file first, then the excavation permit, plus an approved traffic-control plan before touching a main thoroughfare. The environmental clock is usually the longest: Diggers Hotline needs three business days before any dig, and the WDNR stormwater NOI needs 14 working days before an acre of disturbance, which puts roughly three weeks of unavoidable lead in front of a compound or route build. None of these clocks run concurrently by default — sequencing them is the scheduler's job.

seasonality.narrative: Kenosha's build year runs on a southeastern Wisconsin rhythm with a slight lake assist: Lake Michigan delays the first hard freeze along the shoreline and takes the sharpest edge off midwinter, but the clay still freezes deep and the state's road calendar applies in full — frozen-road declarations in winter, Class II thaw postings from late February into spring (2026: February 20 through April 30). The reliable production window is May through October. The clay is the tiebreaker month to month: a wet June site here behaves worse than the rain gauge suggests, and a dry August one better. Confirm the monthly picture against NCEI normals for the Kenosha area before publication — this calendar is authored from the state restriction record plus regional climate pattern, not a station table.

costDrivers.rockNote: With dolomite typically 25–50 ft down, rock almost never enters telecom-depth excavation on the lake plain; the exception risk is isolated shallow-bedrock highs, which borings catch.
costDrivers.spoilDisposalNote: Saturated lake-plain clay spoil hauls heavy and dries slowly; on urban sites with tight footprints, plan export and import rather than assuming reuse.
costDrivers.permitFeeNote: City ROW excavation permits carry pavement degradation fees on top of the base fee — full-depth street cuts price differently than lawn-park bores.
costDrivers.prevailingWageExposure: No state prevailing wage since the 2017 Act 59 repeal took effect. Davis-Bacon still attaches to federally funded scopes, including BEAD builds.
costDrivers.seasonalPremiumNote: Winter concrete protection December through March and the 48-inch embedment are the recurring premiums; spring adds haul-routing cost while local postings are up.
costDrivers.narrative: Cost on a Kenosha civil scope is driven by water management, depth, and timing more than by anything exotic. The clay dictates dewatering, stone working pads, and spoil export on wet sites; the 48-inch frost rule fixes excavation volume on every foundation; and the season decides whether those two facts price normally or with winter protection and thaw-season routing layered on. In the city, ROW degradation fees reward boring over open-cutting streets. One forward-looking driver is competition for resources: the Microsoft program at Mount Pleasant — with a Kenosha campus behind it — is absorbing regional concrete, trucking, and labor capacity, which shows up in lead times before it shows up in prices. We publish drivers, not rates; every estimate here starts from borings and a calendar.

compliance.stateContractorLicensing: Wisconsin has no statewide general contractor license for commercial work — projects are controlled through permits, plan review, and trade credentials instead. Electrical and plumbing carry state licenses; the DSPS Dwelling Contractor credential applies only to 1–2 family residential. Compiled from secondary sources — verify current requirements with DSPS directly.

hazards.designImplications: Winter governs foundations (48-inch embedment) and generator enclosure design, while southeastern Wisconsin's severe-weather season argues for conservative anchorage and hail-tolerant equipment placement. Along the Pike River and lakefront, floodplain screening precedes siting. Publish wind and ice design values only after ASCE hazard and TIA-222 county lookups are completed for this location.

items.headline: Microsoft buys 240 acres in Kenosha for data center development
items.detail: Microsoft purchased 240 acres northwest of the I-94/WIS 142 interchange in January 2025, with concept plans for four single-story 250,000 sq ft data center buildings plus a utility substation; the city rezoned the land and will annex it, though project plans and timeline were not final at announcement.

items.headline: Mount Pleasant campus next door keeps compounding
items.detail: One county north, Microsoft finished its first Mount Pleasant data center (the 'Fairwater' AI supercomputer facility) in June 2026, is building a $4B second facility announced September 2025, and holds approval for 15 more buildings — sustained heavy-civil demand on the same I-94 corridor Kenosha sits on.

items.headline: Wisconsin BEAD: $1.06B approved, three-quarters fiber
items.detail: NTIA approved Wisconsin's final BEAD proposal in December 2025 — $1,055,823,573 administered by the PSC, with roughly 76% of locations awarded to fiber — funding rural fiber construction statewide, including underserved pockets of southeastern Wisconsin.

fiber.narrative: Fiber demand in Kenosha pulls from two directions at once: hyperscale capacity following Microsoft down the I-94 corridor, and last-mile work seeded by Wisconsin's $1.06B BEAD program in the rural western county. The construction realities are specific. City streets sit under a two-step ROW regime — registration before permit, traffic-control plan on main thoroughfares, degradation fees on cuts — which tilts urban routes toward directional boring, and the lake-plain clay bores cleanly when moisture is managed. Two active rail corridors cross the geography: UP's Kenosha Subdivision on the lakefront, where Metra service terminates, and CPKC's Chicago–Milwaukee main to the west. Both are long-lead crossing counterparties; we file crossing applications before route design is final, not after.

primaryScopeIds: small cell and DAS node civil
wireless.narrative: Kenosha's wireless civil market is corridor densification: population growth, logistics parks, and the coming data center workforce all sit along I-94 and the lakeshore, and the sites serving them need pads, power, and grounding built into heavy clay. Every foundation carries Wisconsin's 48-inch frost embedment, so even a small cabinet pad involves real excavation, and winter pours run under full cold-weather protocol. Small-cell and DAS work in the city operates under the statewide Act 14 framework — collocation as a permitted ROW use with the $250 annual cap — rather than a bespoke local ordinance. Delivery logistics favor this market: I-94 stays unposted through thaw season, so spring shelter sets here hinge only on the last-mile local roads, a narrower problem than most Wisconsin markets face.

secondaryScopeIds: heavy haul access and crane pads
edge.narrative: Few Tier 2 markets anywhere have Kenosha's edge trajectory: Microsoft owns 240 acres at I-94 and WIS 142 with a four-building campus in concept plans, and the Mount Pleasant program ten miles north — first facility complete June 2026, $4B second underway, 15 more buildings approved — is already the largest construction program in Wisconsin. That gravity produces exactly the scope tier we self-perform: transformer and switchgear pads, campus conduit and duct bank, generator yards, security compounds, and the micro-edge pads that follow hyperscale capacity into secondary sites. We Energies is the interconnection counterparty, and its queue is filling with data center load — power lead time, not civil production, is the schedule risk we flag first on this corridor.

operations.mobilizationNote: At 234 road miles, Kenosha is a comfortable single-mobilization market for our Cedar Rapids crews: out on US-151 through Dubuque and Madison, then across southern Wisconsin on the interstate network, with crews staying over for the duration of a scope rather than commuting. What makes this market operationally distinctive is the corridor itself — I-94 gives posting-free heavy-haul access straight to most site clusters even in thaw season, so equipment and shelter moves that would wait on rural postings elsewhere in Wisconsin can often proceed here. Multi-site programs across Kenosha County, and combined programs with neighboring Racine County, batch onto one mobilization efficiently. Response-time commitments are made only with ops sign-off.

faq.question: What frost depth applies to telecom foundations in Kenosha?
faq.answer: Wisconsin's SPS 321.16 rule governs: footings bear below the frost line or at least 48 inches below adjacent grade, whichever is deeper. That fixes minimum excavation on every shelter pier, hut footing, and bollard in the county. Confirm the commercial-code application and any local amendment with the city's Building Inspection Division (262-653-4263) during design.

faq.question: Who issues right-of-way permits for underground work in the City of Kenosha?
faq.answer: The Public Works Department, in two steps: a Right-of-Way Registration (form PWE010) must be on file before the excavation permit (form PWE002) will issue. Applications specify which part of the ROW is disturbed, main-thoroughfare work needs a City Engineer-approved traffic-control plan, and pavement cuts carry degradation fees — one reason boring usually beats open-cut on city streets.

faq.question: Is Microsoft actually building a data center in Kenosha?
faq.answer: The land is bought; the buildings aren't final. Microsoft purchased 240 acres northwest of I-94 and WIS 142 in January 2025, the city rezoned it for data center use, and concept plans show four 250,000 sq ft buildings plus a substation — but Microsoft had not finalized project plans or timeline at announcement. The active construction today is at Mount Pleasant, one county north.

faq.question: Do spring road postings delay shelter deliveries around Kenosha?
faq.answer: Less than in most of Wisconsin. The Class II thaw restrictions (2026: February 20 – April 30) apply to posted state highways, and county and town roads add local limits — but I-94 carries legal loads year-round, so the corridor spine stays open. A spring set here usually turns on the final miles of local road, which we scout against current postings before committing a haul date.

faq.question: How much permitting lead time should an underground schedule carry?
faq.answer: Bank three weeks minimum for a disturbance of an acre or more: the WDNR stormwater Notice of Intent must be in 14 working days before ground breaks, and Diggers Hotline requires 3 business days before any excavation. Add the city's two-step ROW process for street work. We run these clocks in parallel wherever the sequence allows so only one of them sits on the critical path.

faq.question: What ground conditions should we expect boring in Kenosha County?
faq.answer: Clayey glacial till and lakebed silts and clays of the Lake Michigan lake plain, with Silurian dolomite typically 25–50 feet down — deep enough that rock rarely enters telecom-depth work. The clay bores predictably at the right moisture but holds water in open cuts and ruts fast under trucking. Site borings settle the question; near the northern lakefront, bluff-edge stability adds a check.

faq.question: How are small cells permitted in the city?
faq.answer: Under the statewide framework of 2019 Wisconsin Act 14 (Wis. Stat. 66.0414), not a city-specific ordinance: small wireless facilities are a permitted use in the ROW, municipal review is constrained, and annual collocation charges cap at the lesser of actual cost or $250 per facility. The civil work — node foundations, conduit, restoration — still runs through the normal Public Works ROW process.

faq.question: Who provides electric service for a new hut or compound in Kenosha?
faq.answer: We Energies, the investor-owned utility serving southeastern Wisconsin. Published new-service timelines don't exist, and the regional queue is absorbing serious data center load, so we treat power lead time as a first-order schedule risk: utility commitment in writing at scoping, and generator-ready designs where the in-service date can't float.

decisionGuidance.heading: Bore or open-cut? How Kenosha's clay and ROW rules decide
decisionGuidance.body: On paper the bore-versus-trench call in Kenosha looks like any urban market's; in practice three local facts stack the deck. First, the city's ROW fee structure charges degradation fees on pavement cuts on top of the base permit, so every foot of open-cut street carries restoration cost that a lawn-park or bore alignment avoids — on a multi-block route that difference compounds fast. Second, the lake-plain clay is a good boring medium at normal moisture: it holds a bore path, doesn't cave like granular soils, and the dolomite is far too deep to interfere. The same clay is a poor open-cut medium in the wet months, when trench walls need boxes, subgrades pump, and spoil turns to export. Third, the corridor's two rail lines — UP's lakefront subdivision and CPKC's main — cross most east–west routes, and a bored crossing is the only realistic option at either. The honest summary: in Kenosha, open-cut earns its place on short laterals, dry-season work, and greenfield edges; anything crossing pavement, rail, or a wet calendar month usually prices and schedules better as a bore. Route design should start from that assumption and let the exceptions prove themselves.
